title: Prologue
body:
*Before I Knew My Name*

There are truths a child is born into long before she is old enough to
understand them.

Mine began with a name.

Not the name people called me. Not the name written on school forms,
church records, or family documents. I mean the other name---the
invisible one. The name that belonged to blood, to origin, to the man
whose face I did not know but whose absence followed me like a shadow.

I was born to a young woman of twenty. My mother was beautiful,
hardworking, and already carrying more than a woman of her age should
have had to carry. My biological father was older, married, and
established in a life that had no proper place for me. By the time I was
born, decisions had already been made by adults who believed silence
could protect everyone.

So I was left with my grandmother.

Later, my mother married the man who would raise me as his own. He gave
me his name. He gave me a place in his house. And for many years, that
was enough for me. Children do not question love when it comes dressed
as routine. A roof. Food on the table. Siblings running through the
house. School uniforms washed and ironed. A father's voice calling
everyone to order.

I did not know then that a family can be both real and not entirely
true.

My mother and the man I called Father made an agreement between
themselves. They would not tell me who I was born from. They would not
speak the name of the man whose blood I carried. Perhaps they thought
they were sparing me confusion. Perhaps they were sparing themselves
shame. Perhaps, like many parents, they believed a secret buried deep
enough becomes a kind of mercy.

But secrets do not die.

They wait.

Mine waited until I was old enough to remember the moment it entered the
room.

# Part One: The House of Many Children

title: Chapter One
body:
*The Father I Knew*

In the beginning, I remember warmth.

Not perfect happiness---life is rarely perfect, even in memory---but
warmth. I remember the noise of a full house, the constant movement of
children, the smell of food, the sharp instructions of adults, and the
comfort of knowing there would always be someone nearby. We were seven
children altogether: three girls and four boys. I was the first child in
the family, though not all the bloodlines in that family ran in the same
direction.

At the time, none of that mattered to me.

The man I called Father was clever, educated, and commanding. To my
young eyes, he seemed to know everything. He had studied widely, spoke
with authority, and carried himself like a man who had seen the world
and understood its inner workings. For a long time, he did not treat me
differently. I belonged to him as much as the others did. At least, that
is how it felt.

My mother worked hard. She was often away because her job required
travel, but when she was home, the house seemed to steady itself. Her
presence could soften the walls. Arguments lowered their voices around
her. Fear, if it was there, knew how to hide.

We were not rich, but we were comfortable. We lived in decent suburbs.
We attended good schools. We had what we needed. I learned early how to
behave, how to study, how to carry myself properly, and how not to ask
unnecessary questions.

Then, when I was still a child, the first crack appeared.

One day, men came to our house looking for Father.

Children are observant witnesses. We may not understand the language of
adults, but we understand tone. We understand when a knock at the door
changes the air. We understand when our mother's face tightens. We
understand when silence becomes frightening.

The men dragged Father out of the house barefoot and without the dignity
he usually wore so well. My mother followed them, shaken and helpless.
They took him away in a vehicle, and when she returned, her eyes were
red. No one explained anything to us that night.

The next morning, we learned enough to know that something serious had
happened. Father had been taken in for offenses we did not understand.
For a while, he was gone. When he returned, he was not the same man, and
neither was our life.

Soon after, we moved.

The new house was smaller. Much smaller. Seven children shared one room,
and the life I had known folded in on itself like a mat being rolled
away. There was no longer space for everyone's restlessness. No corner
where sorrow could sit quietly without being noticed. We slept close
together, our bodies lined up in the dark, breathing each other's air,
listening to the house creak under the weight of everything adults
refused to say.

Children can survive almost anything when they believe it is temporary.

At first, I told myself this was only for a little while. Father would
find his way back to who he had been. Mother would smile again without
effort. We would return to the bigger house, the better life, the
version of ourselves that had lived before the men came.

But some doors close quietly. You only notice they are shut when you try
to walk back through them.

Father changed after that. Or perhaps the change had always been inside
him and hardship simply gave it permission to come out. The commanding
voice I had once admired became sharper. His intelligence, which once
made him seem powerful, began to feel dangerous when turned against us.
He could wound with words. He could make a child feel small without
lifting a hand.

And still, I loved him.

That is one of the hardest truths to explain about childhood. Love does
not disappear simply because fear enters the room. Sometimes they sit
side by side at the same table. Sometimes the same man who buys bread,
pays school fees, and calls you his child is also the man whose
footsteps make your stomach tighten.

I did not know what to do with that contradiction.

So I became good.

Good girls learn quickly. They learn which questions not to ask. They
learn how to hear trouble before it begins. They learn to read faces,
footsteps, silences. They learn when to sweep, when to disappear, when
to comfort younger siblings, when to become invisible.

As the eldest, I carried responsibilities before I had language for
them. I helped with the younger ones. I watched. I listened. I became
another pair of hands for my mother, another set of eyes in the house. I
understood that childhood was not a season granted equally to everyone.
Some children are allowed to play. Others are trained to notice danger.

My mother continued working. She had to. Her strength was not poetic
then; it was practical. It was food. Rent. Uniforms. Transport. Soap.
School books. It was leaving the house even when her heart must have
been tired. It was returning home to seven children and a husband who
had become harder to reach.

Now, when I look back, I understand her differently.

As a girl, I sometimes wondered why she did not explain more, protect
more, speak more. But age has softened my judgment. I know now that many
women survive by dividing themselves. One part goes to work. One part
cooks. One part prays. One part hides fear from the children. One part
keeps a secret so old that it begins to feel like truth.

My mother had many parts.

I only knew the ones she allowed me to see.

In that smaller house, my awareness of difference began to grow. Not
fully. Not yet. But in small, uncomfortable ways. A glance that lasted
too long. A sentence cut short when I entered the room. A relative who
answered one question with another. The feeling of being inside the
family and somehow standing just outside its deepest knowledge.

No one said, You are not his. No one said, There is another man. No one
said, Your name is not the whole story.

Instead, the truth moved around me like wind beneath a door.

I felt it before I knew it.

There were moments when Father's temper seemed to find me differently.
Not always, not openly, not in ways a stranger could easily identify.
But children know when love has conditions. They know when belonging
requires performance. I studied hard. I behaved. I tried to be useful. I
tried to earn the space I occupied.

Perhaps that is where my lifelong hunger for approval began. Or perhaps
it began earlier, at birth, when adults made decisions over my body, my
name, my future, and called it protection.

A child cannot argue with a silence she cannot see.

So I accepted the life I had been given. I wore the name I was given. I
answered when called. I stood in family photographs. I held younger
siblings. I went to school. I prayed. I learned to smile even when I
felt uncertain.

Outside, we looked like a family. Inside, we were becoming something
more complicated.

Still, I must tell the truth with fairness: Father was not only one
thing. No person ever is. He could be stern, yes. Proud. Difficult. At
times frightening. But he could also be generous in the ways he
understood generosity. He believed in education. He wanted his children
to speak well, think well, carry themselves with dignity. He did not
raise us to be foolish. He pushed us because he believed the world would
not be kind to weakness.

There were days when I admired him deeply. There were days when I feared
him. There were days when I needed him. There were days when I wished I
did not.

That is the burden of remembering someone honestly. Memory refuses to
simplify the people who shaped us. It does not allow us to make saints
of them just because they are dead, or villains of them just because
they hurt us. The father I knew was both shelter and storm. He gave me a
name, but not the whole truth. He gave me a place, but not complete
belonging.

And yet, for years, I called him Father without hesitation.

Because he was the one there.

The other man---the man whose blood I carried---was nothing more than a
shadow. I had no face for him. No voice. No smell of his clothes. No
memory of his hand holding mine. He did not teach me to tie my shoes,
did not attend my school meetings, did not call me in from the yard. His
absence was so complete that I mistook it for emptiness.

But absence is not empty. Absence has weight. It sits inside the body
and waits to be named.

As I grew older, I began to feel questions forming in me. They did not
come all at once. They came slowly, cautiously, like someone knocking
from the inside of a locked room.

Why did certain things not make sense? Why did some stories begin after
I had already been born? Why did my mother's face change when certain
names were mentioned? Why did I sometimes feel that everyone knew
something about me except me?

But in our house, questions were dangerous. Questions disturbed the
peace. Questions threatened the structure that held us together. So I
swallowed them.

I became skilled at swallowing.

I swallowed confusion. I swallowed hurt. I swallowed the need to know. I
swallowed anger before I knew it was anger. I swallowed words until they
became stones, and those stones settled somewhere deep in me.

Many years later, I would understand that silence is not the absence of
a story. Silence is often where the story is buried.

Back then, I was only a girl trying to survive the weather inside our
home.

The smaller house taught me many lessons. It taught me that comfort can
vanish. That adults can fall. That shame can move a family from one
place to another without announcing itself. It taught me that children
often inherit consequences before they inherit explanations.

It also taught me endurance.

We endured the crowded room. We endured the change in Father. We endured
Mother's absences and returns. We endured the feeling that life had once
been larger and had now been reduced to something we had to squeeze
ourselves into.

And still, we laughed sometimes.

That, too, must be remembered.

Even in difficult houses, children laugh. We played. We teased one
another. We fought over space and food and small privileges. We created
worlds out of nothing. We turned hardship into games because that is
what children do when they are not yet ready to call hardship by its
name.

There were moments of light.

A shared joke in the dark. A sibling's foot pressing against mine while
we slept. The smell of something cooking when there had been worry about
food. My mother's hand smoothing my hair. A school prize. A Sunday
morning. A song from church rising above everything we could not say.

Faith entered my life early, though not always as comfort. Sometimes
faith was discipline. Sometimes it was fear. Sometimes it was the
language adults used when they had no answers. But even then, something
in me wanted to believe that God saw what people hid. That He knew names
before human beings changed them. That He could read the secret places
where children stored their pain.

Maybe that belief saved me. Maybe it only gave me somewhere to put my
longing.

What I know is this: the house of many children was the first place I
learned how divided a heart can be.

I loved my mother, but I did not fully know her. I loved my father, but
I was afraid of him. I loved my siblings, but even among them, I
sometimes felt alone. I loved the name I carried, because it was mine.

And yet somewhere beneath it, another name waited.

At the time, I did not know that my life would become a journey of
crossing borders---not only between countries, but between truths. I did
not know I would one day leave homes, marriages, familiar languages, and
old versions of myself. I did not know that motherhood would reopen
wounds I thought childhood had closed. I did not know that grief would
follow me, or that faith would later become less of an inheritance and
more of a choice.

I only knew that something in me was watching. Something in me was
remembering.

Even before I understood the secret, my spirit had begun keeping record.

And perhaps that is where this story truly begins---not with the man who
gave me his name, nor the man whose name was hidden from me, but with
the child I was between them.

A child in a crowded room. A child listening through walls. A child
learning that love and truth are not always introduced at the same time.

A child who did not yet know her whole name, but who had already begun
the long work of becoming herself.

title: Chapter Two
body:
*The Girl Who Learned to Listen*

Childhood did not arrive in one clear shape. It came in pieces: school
mornings and church songs, crowded bedrooms and polished shoes, the
smell of starch on uniforms, the scrape of chairs across a floor, the
sound of my mother leaving before the house had fully woken.

When I try to remember myself as a young girl, I do not first see my
face. I see my hands.

Small hands rinsing cups. Small hands holding a younger child. Small
hands smoothing a skirt before school. Small hands learning, earlier
than they should have, that usefulness could be mistaken for goodness.

I was the first child in the house, and that position carried a kind of
invisible crown. It did not shine. It weighed. Being first meant I was
watched more closely, corrected more sharply, expected to understand
things no one had explained. When something went missing, I was asked.
When a younger child cried, I was called. When the house needed order,
my name rose quickly to the surface.

There are children who grow up believing the world is waiting to welcome
them. I grew up believing the world was testing me.

In school, I learned a different kind of discipline. There were rules
for sitting, rules for speaking, rules for handwriting, rules for how a
girl should carry herself. I liked books because books had beginnings
and endings. They did not whisper behind closed doors. They did not
change their story depending on who was in the room. If I opened a page,
the words stayed where they were.

That steadiness comforted me.

I worked hard because school gave me something home could not always
give: a place where effort made sense. If I studied, I could pass. If I
listened, I could answer. If I kept my uniform clean and my books neat,
adults praised me. Praise became a language I learned quickly. It was
safer than need. Neater than longing. Easier to hold than questions.

But even at school, I carried the house with me.

I carried the memory of Father's voice. I carried my mother's tired
eyes. I carried the crowded room and the feeling that there was never
enough space to be fully alone. I carried the secret before I knew it
was a secret. It sat beneath my skin like a second heartbeat.

Children do not need facts to recognize tension. They recognize it in
pauses, in glances, in the way adults become careful around certain
topics. I began to notice that some conversations bent away from me.
Names would appear and disappear. A story would begin, then someone
would remember I was present and fold it shut.

At family gatherings, I watched faces. I learned that grown people often
spoke twice: once with their mouths and once with their eyes. The mouth
might say, "Go and play," but the eyes said, "You were not meant to hear
that." The mouth might laugh, but the eyes carried warning. I became
fluent in that silent language.

My grandmother remained a figure of deep importance in the background of
my life. She belonged to my earliest beginning, to a time before memory.
I knew I had been left with her as a baby, but as a child I did not yet
understand the size of that leaving. Babies do not remember being placed
in another woman's arms. But the body remembers what the mind cannot
organize. Perhaps that is why I often felt a strange ache when women
said goodbye. Perhaps that is why departures troubled me, even ordinary
ones.

My mother's departures were the most familiar.

Because of her work, she travelled, and each time she left, the house
shifted. I would watch her prepare, gathering clothes and necessities,
becoming practical so she would not become emotional. She had a way of
moving quickly when she did not want to feel too much. I see that now.
At the time, I only saw the bag, the doorway, the leaving.

I wanted to ask her to stay. I wanted to ask when she would return. I
wanted to ask whether she thought of me when she was away. Instead, I
tried to be sensible. Eldest daughters are often praised for being
sensible when what they really are is afraid to make things harder.

When she came back, I studied her mood before approaching. If she was
happy, I moved closer. If she was quiet, I waited. If there was strain
between her and Father, I became careful. The house taught me timing. It
taught me that love sometimes needed permission to be received.

My siblings were my first community and my first mirror. With them, I
could be bossy, protective, jealous, playful, tired. We fought over
blankets and food and whose turn it was to do something. We laughed at
jokes that would not have been funny outside that room, but inside it
they became medicine. We knew how to irritate one another and how to
defend one another. In a crowded childhood, privacy was rare, but
companionship was constant.

There were nights when all of us lay in the same room, each pretending
to be asleep while the adults spoke elsewhere in the house. We listened
without moving. A child learns to breathe quietly when she wants to hear
what she is not allowed to know.

Sometimes the conversations were ordinary: money, school, relatives,
church, work. Other times the words blurred into tones---anger,
pleading, accusation, fatigue. The details escaped me, but the feeling
remained. Feelings are often the first archive of childhood.

I remember food by its emotional temperature. Some meals felt peaceful,
with plates passed around and someone laughing. Other meals felt tight,
each of us aware that one wrong word could sharpen the air. I learned to
eat quickly without seeming greedy, to accept what was given, to say
thank you, to read whether second helpings were possible or foolish to
ask for.

I remember clothes, too. Uniforms mattered. Shoes mattered. Hair
mattered. Respectability mattered. My mother understood that the world
judges children through the appearance of their mothers, and mothers
through the appearance of their children. No matter what was happening
inside the house, we were expected to look cared for. Clean collars.
Neat hems. Proper manners. We might have shared a room, but we would not
carry disorder into the street.

That insistence on dignity shaped me. It taught me pride, but it also
taught me concealment. I learned that pain could be combed smooth,
buttoned up, and sent outside with polished shoes.

Church was another place where I learned to perform and to hope. The
singing stirred something in me. Music could lift the roof off a room.
It could make sorrow sound beautiful without denying that it was sorrow.
I listened to prayers and sermons, to talk of obedience, forgiveness,
suffering, and blessing. Some words frightened me. Some words comforted
me. Some words took years to understand.

As a girl, I thought faith meant being good enough for God to notice.
Later, I would learn that faith was also crying when no one else could
hear, asking questions that sounded too dangerous for daylight, and
still waking up the next morning.

There were small pleasures in my childhood, and I want to honor them.
Memory must not become so loyal to pain that it erases joy.

I remember the thrill of new exercise books. The clean smell of
untouched pages. I remember the pride of writing my name carefully on
the front, each letter a claim: this belongs to me. I remember playing
outside until someone called us in. I remember the strange happiness of
borrowed things, shared sweets, songs learned from other children, the
warmth of sitting close to someone during a cold evening.

I remember wanting to be seen.

Not watched. Seen.

There is a difference. To be watched is to be monitored. To be seen is
to be known. Much of my childhood was spent under watchful eyes, but the
deeper parts of me remained hidden even from myself. I did not yet have
the courage to say, "Something feels unfinished in me." I did not know
how to say, "Why do I feel like I am waiting for a truth no one wants to
give me?"

So I became a girl of surfaces and depths. On the surface, I was
capable. I was the eldest. I was a student. I was a daughter. I was a
sister. I was the child who helped. Beneath the surface, I was listening
for my own beginning.

Sometimes I wondered whether other children felt as I did. Did they also
sense rooms changing when they entered? Did they also lie awake trying
to arrange adult fragments into a story? Did they also feel guilty for
wanting answers?

I did not ask.

Questions, in our house, were not always invitations. Sometimes they
were accusations. Sometimes they opened doors adults had spent years
holding shut.

One of the hardest parts of being a child in a family with secrets is
that you often become loyal to the very silence that hurts you. You
protect the adults by pretending not to notice. You protect the house by
becoming easy to manage. You protect yourself by accepting half-answers
because full answers might cost too much.

But the self is patient.

It waits beneath obedience. It waits beneath fear. It waits beneath the
borrowed name, the family photograph, the school report, the church
dress, the chores, the laughter, the swallowed tears. It waits for one
moment of permission.

Mine had not yet come.

Still, there were signs that the truth was alive.

I would catch my mother looking at me sometimes with an expression I
could not read. It was not ordinary tenderness. It carried apology,
memory, perhaps even fear. When I asked what was wrong, she would look
away or say nothing was wrong. Nothing was a word adults used often, and
I learned early that nothing could mean everything.

There were relatives who loved me but handled me carefully, as if I were
a cup with a crack no one wanted to mention. Some were kind in ways that
felt weighted. Some avoided too much closeness. Some seemed to know
where the invisible lines were and never crossed them. I began to
understand that families are maps, and some roads are deliberately left
unnamed.

The man I called Father remained central to the map. His name covered
us. His authority arranged the house. Even when he was absent, he
occupied space. When he was pleased, everyone breathed more freely. When
he was displeased, the walls seemed to draw nearer.

I wanted his approval. This is another truth I must tell plainly. Even
when I sensed a distance, even when I feared his anger, I wanted him to
be proud of me. I wanted to be chosen by the man whose name I carried. I
wanted the name to be enough.

But children cannot make adults whole by being good.

No report card, no obedience, no silence, no careful smile can repair
what a family refuses to face. I did not know that then, so I kept
trying.

Looking back, I see a girl standing between two inheritances. One
inheritance was visible: the family that raised me, the siblings beside
me, the father whose name I used, the mother whose love was braided with
secrecy and survival. The other inheritance was hidden: blood, origin,
unanswered questions, a man whose absence had shaped my life without
permission.

I lived inside both, though I could name only one.

That is why childhood, for me, was not simply a place I passed through.
It was a room full of doors. Some were open: school, church, chores,
siblings, responsibility. Some were locked: my beginning, my father's
name, my mother's full story. I moved among the open doors and learned
not to touch the locked ones.

Yet every locked door has a sound behind it.

By the time I was old enough to notice myself noticing, I had already
become a keeper of fragments. I kept the sound of my mother's suitcase.
I kept Father's changed voice. I kept my siblings' laughter in the dark.
I kept the smell of soap and starch. I kept the feeling of a house
pretending to be ordinary.

Most of all, I kept my questions.

They were not loud yet. They did not yet demand answers. They simply
lived in me, small and persistent, like seeds under dry ground.

One day, they would break through.

But before that day came, I had to grow. I had to learn the language of
endurance. I had to become useful, watchful, faithful, afraid, hopeful.
I had to become the kind of girl who could survive not knowing.

And I did survive.

Not because I was untouched, but because something in me refused to
disappear. Even when I did not know my whole name, I knew I existed.
Even when adults chose silence, my spirit chose memory. Even when I was
given only fragments, some deeper part of me believed that fragments
could one day become a story.

This is that story.

The story of a girl who learned to read rooms before books could save
her. The story of a daughter who loved a mother she could not fully
understand. The story of a child who carried a borrowed certainty while
an unnamed truth waited beneath it.

The story of how, before I knew my name, I learned to listen for myself.
